edges.description: IL-1 is the prototypic endogenous pyrogen, and fever is the single most commonly reported symptom.
Venous thrombosis occurs in this disease, and systemic inflammation is the presumed route. No source here establishes the intervening mechanism.
Pulmonary involvement is catalogued among the manifestations. Whether it is sterile inflammatory or infective is not distinguished in these sources.
Unopposed IL-1 signalling in bone produces multifocal sterile osteomyelitis with periosteal reaction.

Breathlessness is counted separately from pneumonia in the review and is more common than it, so it is not simply a manifestation of the pneumonia. No cached source establishes the route from systemic inflammation to breathlessness.

Growth retardation in a disease presenting in the first months of life. Chronic interleukin-1 driven inflammation is the plausible route, but no cached source establishes the mechanism, so the intermediates are left unstated.

Raised white cell count as a direct readout of the unopposed interleukin-1 signalling, not of infection. The distinction matters because the sterile lesions are routinely treated as infection before the diagnosis is reached.

Anaemia of chronic inflammation. The intermediate is the sustained acute phase response, and the pooled anakinra analysis showing haemoglobin recovery on treatment is what supports the link being inflammatory rather than nutritional.
The same unopposed signalling in skin produces generalised pustulosis.
The bone lesion as diagnosed clinically and radiologically.
Periosteal reaction accompanying the osteomyelitis, and part of the defining triad.
Osteolytic lesions weaken bone sufficiently to fracture, one of the osteoarticular manifestations catalogued in the systematic review.
Joint pain from the same sterile inflammatory process, counted alongside the other osteoarticular manifestations.
Contracture follows joint and periarticular inflammation, but no cached source traces the sequence, so the intermediates are left unstated rather than assumed.
The same sterile inflammatory process resorbs bone, producing the osteolytic lesions catalogued alongside fracture and osteomyelitis in the osteoarticular group.
The cutaneous lesion as observed, the third element of the defining triad.

Nail changes are catalogued as a manifestation but no cached source describes the nail histology or establishes that the same neutrophilic process reaches the nail unit, so the intermediates between skin inflammation and nail change are left unstated.

edges.description: Confirms that losing IL-1Ra alone is sufficient to produce spontaneous inflammatory disease, which is the core claim of the human mechanism.
edges.limitations: The organ targeted differs from the human disease and differs between mouse strains, giving arthritis or vasculitis rather than sterile osteomyelitis and pustulosis. The model therefore supports the sufficiency of IL-1Ra loss to cause inflammation without reproducing the tissue distribution that defines the human condition.

nodes.description: Nail changes in 41.37 percent of the pooled cohort. Every source says "nail changes" without describing morphology, so the binding is to the general abnormal-morphology term. Nail dystrophy would assert dystrophy specifically, which no source here does.

nodes.description: The initiating lesion. Homozygous or compound heterozygous IL1RN variants abolish or truncate the interleukin-1 receptor antagonist. Point mutations, frameshifts and genomic deletions all occur, including a Puerto Rican deletion removing IL1RN together with five other IL-1 family members and a 22 kb deletion spanning the first four exons.

nodes.description: A recombinant fusion protein that acts as a soluble decoy receptor, binding both IL-1 alpha and IL-1 beta. That dual binding matches the defect here better than canakinumab does, since both ligands are left unopposed when the antagonist is absent. It is named as one of three IL-1 blockers used in this disease, but the cached sources report no outcome data for it in DIRA specifically. Modality is recorded as OTHER because a decoy-receptor fusion protein is neither a monoclonal antibody nor replacement of a protein the patient lacks.
